entry: Italian-Spanish cardinal deacon and condottiero. He was the illegitimate son of [[Pope Alexander VI]] and sibling of Lucrezia Borgia. Made a cardinal at 18 after his father's election to the papacy, he resigned on August 17, 1498, to pursue a military career, and Louis XII of France named him duke of Valentinois the same day. As a condottiero for Louis around 1500, he occupied [[Milan]] and [[Naples]] during the [[Italian Wars]] and carved out a state in central Italy. He was unable to retain power for long after his father's death. Several contemporaries suggested that he had killed his brother Giovanni in 1497, but his role in the act has never been clear. His quest for power is documented in [[Niccolò Machiavelli]]'s treatise *The Prince*.

American four-seat, single-engine, high-wing [[Fixed-wing aircraft|fixed-wing]] general aviation aircraft. First flown in 1955, it was developed from the Cessna 170 and has tricycle landing gear. The first production model was delivered in 1956. More 172s have been built than any other aircraft, with more than 44,000 units. After a break in production beginning in 1986, the aircraft remains in production.

Class of parasitic [[Flatworm|flatworms]] in the phylum Platyhelminthes, commonly known as tapeworms. Most species, including the best known, belong to the subclass Eucestoda, whose adults are ribbon-like and whose bodies consist of segments called proglottids, which are packages of eggs shed into the environment. The subclass Cestodaria consists mainly of fish parasites. Many cestodes have complex life histories with one or two intermediate hosts in which the [[Larva|larvae]] develop. Adults typically live in the digestive tracts of [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]]. Some six thousand species have been described. Tapeworms attach to the intestine with a scolex armed with hooks or suckers, and they absorb nutrients directly from the host's gut. Humans can be infected by eating undercooked pork, beef or fish.

Infraorder of marine [[Mammal|mammals]] that includes [[Whale|whales]], [[Dolphin|dolphins]] and [[Porpoise|porpoises]]. Cetaceans have fully aquatic life cycles, streamlined fish-like bodies and tail flukes, and they must surface to breathe. Toothed whales use echolocation. About 90 living species are recognized, 75 toothed whales (Odontoceti) and 15 baleen whales (Mysticeti). The [[Blue whale]] is the largest animal known to have existed, with a maximum confirmed length of 29.9 meters (98 feet). Genetic and fossil evidence place cetaceans within the [[Artiodactyla|even-toed ungulates]], most closely related to hippopotamids. Cetaceans were extensively hunted for meat, blubber and oil after the Industrial Revolution. Although the International Whaling Commission agreed to halt [[Whaling|commercial whaling]], hunting continues under quotas and for scientific research.

Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordered by [[Morocco]] and lying between the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. [[Phoenicia|Phoenicians]] founded a settlement there. Portugal annexed it in 1415, and in 1580 it passed to the Hispanic Monarchy; the city chose to remain under Spanish authority after 1640. It became an autonomous city in March 1995. Ceuta is part of the [[Schengen Area]], with border checks between it and European Spain. Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty, which Spain upholds.

Traditional cold dish of raw fish or shellfish marinated in citrus and seasonings. It is found across coastal [[Latin America|Latin American]] countries on the [[Pacific Ocean]], and is the national dish of [[Peru]]. [[UNESCO]] recognizes it as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The acid makes the flesh opaque and firm, but the seafood remains raw. The marinade typically uses [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] or lemon juice, [[Chili pepper|chili]], onion and cilantro. It is eaten as an appetizer or with starchy sides such as [[Sweet potato]] or [[Maize|maize]]. The word ceviche is first documented in 1820.

Landlocked country in [[Central Africa]]. Its capital and largest city is [[N'Djamena]], and its population is 20 million. It covers 1,300,000 sq km (500,000 sq mi), the fifth-largest country in Africa. French and Arabic are the official languages, and more than 200 ethnic and linguistic groups live there. [[Islam]] (55.1%) and [[Christianity]] (41.1%) are the main religions. [[France]] conquered the territory by 1920, and Chad gained independence in 1960. A civil war erupted in 1965. Idriss Déby overthrew President Hissène Habré in 1990. After Déby was killed by rebels in April 2021, a Transitional Military Council led by his son Mahamat Déby took control. Since 2003 crude oil has been the main source of export earnings, and Chad ranks the 4th lowest in the [[Human Development Index]].

Serial assembly of connected links, typically of metal. Like a [[Rope|rope]], a chain is flexible and curved in compression but linear, rigid and load-bearing in tension. Chains designed for lifting, pulling or securing have torus-shaped links that bend in two dimensions. Chains for transferring power in machines have links that mesh with sprocket teeth and bend in only one dimension; these are known as roller chains. Bicycle chains transfer power from the pedals to the drive wheel, and timing chains transfer rotation from the crankshaft to an engine's valves and ignition system. Uses range from jewelry and [[Chain mail]] to [[Chainsaw|chainsaws]]. Two chains may be joined with a quick link, carabiner or shackle.

Personal [[Armour|armor]] of small metal rings linked together in a pattern to form a mesh. Mail was widely used in European militaries from the 3rd century BC to the 16th century AD, and in Asia, Africa and the Middle East until the 18th century. A coat of mail is often called a hauberk. The earliest surviving examples, dated to the 3rd century BC, were found in the Carpathian Basin, and its invention is commonly credited to the [[Celts]]. Its use declined in the 16th and 17th centuries as [[Plate armour|plate armor]] and more advanced [[Firearm|firearms]] were developed. Mail is still used in industries such as butchery and as protection against the bites of [[Shark|sharks]].

Formula in [[Calculus|calculus]] for differentiating the composition of two differentiable functions. If z depends on y, and y depends on x, the derivative of z with respect to x is the product of the derivatives dz/dy and dy/dx, so that dz/dx = dz/dy · dy/dx. In integration, the counterpart of the chain rule is the substitution rule. The rule seems to have first been used by [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]], who also devised its common notation.

Portable handheld power [[Saw|saw]] that cuts with teeth attached to a [[Chain|chain]] rotating along a guide bar. Modern chainsaws are typically gasoline or electric and are used for tree felling, pruning, firewood harvesting, and cutting concrete and ice. A chainsaw comprises an engine, a drive mechanism, a guide bar, a cutting chain, a tensioning mechanism and safety features. Its precursors were first used in surgery, where Scottish doctors John Aitken and James Jeffray pioneered a flexible chain saw around 1783–1785. Patents for wood chainsaws began in the late 19th century. The first portable chainsaw was developed and patented in 1918 by Canadian millwright James Shand.

Seat typically designed for one person, with one or more legs, a flat or slightly angled seat and a back rest. It may be made of [[Wood|wood]], [[Metal|metal]] or synthetic materials, and may be padded or upholstered. An armchair has fixed armrests; a recliner has a mechanism that lowers the back and raises a footrest; a rocking chair has legs fixed to two curved slats; and a [[Wheelchair|wheelchair]] has wheels fixed to an axis under the seat. Chairs have been used since antiquity, but for centuries they were a symbol of state and dignity rather than ordinary furniture. Chairs became common only in the 16th century, when people had sat on chests, benches and stools. The chair is still used as an emblem of authority in the House of Commons of the [[United Kingdom]] and [[Canada]].

Indian Hindu saint from [[Bengal]] who founded Gaudiya Vaishnavism. He is often considered an incarnation of [[Krishna]], and some regard him as the combined [[Avatar|avatar]] of Radha and Krishna. His worship of Krishna through devotional singing (bhajan-kirtan) and dance influenced [[Vaishnavism]] in Bengal. He popularized chanting of the Hare Krishna Maha-mantra and composed the Shikshashtakam, eight devotional prayers. He is considered the chief proponent of the Vedantic philosophy of achintya-bhedabheda, an inconceivable difference in non-difference. He is sometimes called Gauranga or Gaura because of his molten gold-like complexion. Hagiographies of the Gaudiya tradition are the only sources for the reconstruction of his life.

American singer and songwriter known as the Queen of [[Funk]]. She was the lead vocalist of the funk band Rufus from the early 1970s, with hits including "Tell Me Something Good" and "Ain't Nobody." Her debut solo album featured the R&B number-one "I'm Every Woman." Her 1984 cover of [[Prince (musician)|Prince]]'s "I Feel for You" made her the first R&B artist to have a crossover hit featuring a rapper. She has won 11 [[Grammy Awards]]. She was named an inductee of the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2023, in the Musical Excellence category.

Psychic or psychospiritual energy center in the subtle body, used as a [[Meditation|meditation]] aid. Visualized in [[Hinduism|Hindu]] and [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] tantric [[Yoga|yoga]], chakras are mentioned in medieval Buddhist texts from the 8th century CE as four or five in number. The best-known system has seven chakras, described in Arthur Avalon's 1919 book *The Serpent Power*. Modern Western occultism regards chakras as actual, though esoteric, energy centers. This view arose in the 1880s with [[Helena Blavatsky]] and other Theosophists.

Microcrystalline or cryptocrystalline form of silica, composed mainly of [[Quartz|quartz]] with minor amounts of intergrown moganite. It has a waxy luster and is semitransparent or translucent. Common colors are white to gray, grayish-blue and brown, and commercial material is often dyed or heated to enhance its color. The name may derive from Chalcedon, a town in Asia Minor, though the Online Etymology Dictionary calls this connection "very doubtful." [[Pliny the Elder]] used the name for a translucent kind of [[Jasper|jasper]].

Archaeological period, also called the Copper Age or Eneolithic, that followed the [[Neolithic]] and preceded the [[Bronze Age]]. It was marked by increasing use of [[Smelting|smelted]] [[Copper|copper]], although stone tools were still predominant. Cold hammering of near-pure copper ore began around 6,500 BC, as in the Great Lakes Old Copper complex of North America. At Belovode in [[Serbia]] has been found the world's oldest securely dated evidence of high-temperature copper smelting, from c. 5,000 BC. In Europe the transition to the Bronze Age occurred between the late 5th and late 3rd millennium BC. In Britain the Chalcolithic lasted from about 2,500 to 2,200 BC, a short period marked by the first copper and gold objects.

Region, probably in the marshy land of southern [[Mesopotamia]]. West Semitic-speaking migrants from the [[Levant]] arrived between the 11th and 9th centuries BC. The Kaldu, later known as Chaldeans, settled chiefly on the left bank of the [[Euphrates]] in the far southeast of [[Babylonia]]. Strictly, Chaldea was the plain formed by the Euphrates and [[Tigris]] deposits, about 640 kilometers (400 mi) long and averaging 160 km (100 mi) wide, although Hebrew literature used the name loosely for all of southern Mesopotamia. A Chaldean dynasty ruled Babylonia from 626 BC to 539 BC, at the height of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. The Chaldeans should not be confused with the modern Chaldean Catholic Church, whose adherents are predominantly ethnic Assyrians.

Soft, white, porous sedimentary carbonate rock, a form of [[Limestone]]. It is composed mainly of [[Calcite|calcite]] from the shells of [[Plankton|plankton]] that settled on the sea floor. In Western Europe it formed during the Late [[Cretaceous]] and early Paleocene. Steep cliffs at Dover, on the [[Kent]] coast, mark where it meets the [[English Channel]]. Mined for quicklime, bricks and putty, chalk is also used to raise the pH of acidic soils.

Deepest known point of Earth's [[Seabed|seabed]], at the southern end of the [[Mariana Trench]] in the western [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]]. A 2021 study put its depth at 10,935 ± 6 meters (35,876 ± 20 feet). It was named after the British Royal Navy survey ship *HMS Challenger*, whose 1872–1876 expedition first located it. The first descent, made by the U.S. Navy's bathyscaphe *Trieste*, took place in January 1960. As of July 2022, 27 people had descended to the Challenger Deep.

Form of [[Classical music|classical music]] written for a small group of instruments, with one performer to each part. Traditionally it was written for a group that could fit in a palace chamber or a large room, and it usually excludes solo performance. For more than 100 years it was played mainly by amateurs in their homes, and it requires musical and social skills different from those of solo or orchestral playing. [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe|Goethe]] described a string quartet as "four rational people conversing," an analogy for the way one instrument introduces a melody that others answer. In the [[Baroque]] era, trio sonatas gave equal importance to their three instruments, and works such as *The Art of Fugue* by [[Johann Sebastian Bach]] could be played on keyboard or by a string quartet. The string quartet, with two violins, viola and cello, became the most prominent form.

Family of Old World [[Lizard|lizards]], best known for color-changing [[Camouflage|camouflage]]. Chameleons have zygodactylous feet, a prehensile tail and independently mobile eyes, and they catch [[Insect|insects]] with projectile tongues. Typically arboreal, they live in habitats from rainforest to desert. The vast majority occur in Africa, and about half of the species are restricted to [[Madagascar]]; a few live across southern Asia as far east as India and Sri Lanka. Their color change arises from layers of skin cells, including iridophores containing guanine nanocrystals. Although the change is often described as camouflage, studies also link it to social communication. Chameleons have been introduced to [[Hawaii]] and [[Florida]].

Collection of independent Cham states along the coast of central and southern [[Vietnam]], from the 2nd century AD until 1832. Early Champa evolved from the seafaring Sa Huỳnh culture. [[Hinduism]], adopted through conflict and conquest of territory from neighboring Funan in the 4th century AD, shaped its art and culture, including red brick temples. Champa reached its height in the 9th and 10th centuries CE. Its trade networks linked the [[Indian Ocean]] with East Asia until the 17th century, when pressure from the Vietnamese polity centered at [[Hanoi]] caused a gradual decline. In 1832 Emperor Minh Mạng of the [[Nguyễn dynasty]] annexed the remaining territories. Many Cham people now adhere to [[Islam]], a conversion that began in the 10th century.

Semi-legendary Brahmin adviser of [[Chandragupta Maurya|Chandragupta]], the first Mauryan emperor. Legendary narratives from traditions dating from the 4th to 11th century CE say that he helped Chandragupta rise to power and helped establish the [[Maurya Empire]], serving as chief adviser to Chandragupta and to his son Bindusara. He is conventionally identified with Kauṭilya, also called Vishnugupta, the author of the *Arthashastra*. That treatise is now thought, with high probability, to have been composed by several authors in the early centuries CE, and its attribution to Chanakya may have been meant to add prestige. There is no documented historical information about him.

Union territory and city in northwestern [[India]], serving as the shared capital of [[Punjab|Punjab]] and [[Haryana]]. It was established after the 1947 partition, when Lahore was ceded to [[Pakistan]] and East Punjab needed a new capital. A masterplan for the modernist city was prepared by Swiss-French architect [[Le Corbusier]], and its initial phases were built in the 1950s and 1960s. A 1966 reorganization created Haryana and Punjab, with Chandigarh as a union territory serving as their joint capital, and its status has remained disputed. The Capitol Complex, the culmination of Le Corbusier's career, was designated a [[World Heritage Site]] by UNESCO in 2016 as part of his buildings. The tri-city area has a combined population of over 1,611,770.
